Philip Roth. Born in nineteen thirty-three, died in two thousand eighteen, he was an American novelist whose fiction explores Jewish identity, sexuality, and the mythologies of America with provocative irony and metafictional sophistication. His work ranges from realist family sagas to elaborate satirical fantasies, but all turn on the collision between individual desire and collective expectation. He stands among the most decorated American writers of the late twentieth century.

Portnoy's Complaint arrived in nineteen sixty-nine as a scandalous comic monologue of a Jewish man's sexual neurosis and oedipal rebellion—it became a cultural watershed that couldn't be ignored. The Plot Against America, his nineteen eighty-four novel, presents an alternate history where Charles Lindbergh becomes US President, exploring antisemitism and American authoritarianism. American Pastoral, published in nineteen ninety-seven, is a tragic bildungsroman of a Jewish businessman undone by his daughter's radicalism, winning the Pulitzer Prize. He also created the Zuckerman tetralogy spanning nineteen seventy-six to nineteen eighty-eight, featuring an alter-ego writer tracking American obsessions across decades.

Roth won the National Book Award twice and was shortlisted for the Pulitzer Prize four times—one of literature's most nominated figures. He pioneered metafictional play in American realism, with characters debating the author's motives and stories within stories destabilizing truth claims. He wrote about sexuality and bodily existence with unprecedented explicitness, reshaping the bounds of American letters.

His work engages deeply with identity itself: what does it mean to be American, Jewish, a writer? He shares territory with elder modernist Saul Bellow whose influence shaped him, and with Norman Mailer as a contemporary novelist of American transgression. His reflexive narrative strategies reshaped how we read both authority and identity.
